concept.name: Heaps & Priority Queues
concept.tagline: Maintain dynamic min/max order with O(log n) inserts and O(1) peek for top-K, scheduling, and graph algorithms.

spark.summary: A binary heap stores elements in a complete tree where each parent is smaller (min-heap) or larger (max-heap) than its children, enabling efficient priority queue operations.
spark.keyTakeaway: Use a heap when you need repeated access to the current best element—top-K, Dijkstra, or task scheduling—not when you need full sorted order.

concept.whyItMatters: Many interview and production problems reduce to “always know the next best item” without sorting the entire collection on every step.
whenNotToUse: Need fully sorted output of all elements upfront
Tiny fixed-size arrays where sort is simpler
keyPoints: Heapify builds a heap in O(n)
Priority queue API maps cleanly to min/max heaps

examples.title: Top-K streaming counts
examples.scenario: Track the 10 hottest product SKUs from a high-volume click stream.
examples.outcome: Min-heap of size K avoids sorting millions of keys on every window.

tradeOffs.con: No efficient search for arbitrary keys

commonMistakes: Using sort() when only top-K is needed
Confusing heap with hash map for membership

deepDive.markdownContent:
## Heap mechanics

Heaps are typically stored in arrays with index arithmetic for parent/child navigation. Priority queues power Dijkstra, Huffman coding, and OS schedulers.

caseStudy.impact: Sub-millisecond peek of the next due job

relationships.description: Dijkstra relies on a min-priority queue.
Top-K is a common coding pattern solved with heaps.
